assessment.title: Data Structures Mini-Assessment
assessment.subject: Computer Science
assessment.instructions: Answer every question. Multiple-select questions state their scoring policy.

questions.prompt: Which data structure follows first-in, first-out order?
Select all data structures that support efficient search for a key under their usual assumptions.
Define a hash collision and describe one consequence for a hash table.
Compare arrays and linked lists with respect to random access, insertion, and memory overhead. Explain how the differences influence a design decision.

q1.explanation: A queue processes elements in FIFO order.

q2.explanation: Merge sort and quicksort compare elements, unlike counting sort and radix sort.

q3.explanation: Hash tables have expected constant-time lookup and balanced search trees have logarithmic lookup; unsorted linear collections require linear search.

q4.reference_answer: A collision occurs when distinct keys produce the same hash value or index/bucket. Collision handling such as chaining or probing is required, and collisions can increase lookup time.

criteria.description: Defines a collision correctly. Full credit: States that distinct keys can map to the same hash value or bucket.
Explains a relevant consequence. Full credit: Explains how collisions require resolution or can impair table performance.

q5.reference_answer: Arrays typically provide constant-time indexed access and contiguous memory; linked lists require traversal for indexed access. Linked-list insertion is constant time only once the location is known, while middle-array insertion requires shifting; resizing may also be relevant. Linked lists have pointer overhead; arrays typically have better locality. The best choice depends on workload and constraints.

criteria.description: Compares random access accurately. Full credit: Contrasts array indexing with linked-list traversal correctly.
Compares insertion and memory overhead accurately. Full credit: Explains relevant insertion qualifications and memory differences.
Justifies a design choice for a specific workload. Full credit: Links an explicit workload to the appropriate access, insertion or memory tradeoffs.

assessment.title: Proportional Reasoning Mini-Assessment
assessment.subject: Quantitative Reasoning
assessment.instructions: Answer every question. The multiple-select question states its scoring policy. The short answer is marked against a five-criterion rubric; the grader may award any fraction of the five points, justified against each criterion's description.

questions.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of milk. Which expression gives the amount of flour needed for 7 cups of milk?
Which of the following are legitimate ways to test whether two quantities are proportional?

options.text: Check whether the ratio of the two quantities is constant across data pairs.
Check whether the graph passes through the origin.
Check whether a single pair of values has a ratio greater than one.
Check whether the differences between successive values are constant.

questions.prompt: A car travels 240 km in 3 hours. Assuming a constant speed, explain how you would find the distance travelled in 7.5 hours, carry out the calculation, and state what the result means.

q1.explanation: The rate is flour per milk, 3/2, so 7 cups of milk require 7 × (3/2) = 10.5 cups of flour.

q2.explanation: A constant ratio and an origin-crossing graph both characterise proportionality; a single pair's ratio and constant successive differences do not.

q3.reference_answer: Speed = 240/3 = 80 km/h; distance = 80 × 7.5 = 600 km. The result says the car covers 600 km if the speed stays constant.

criteria.description: Identifies the constant rate that the proportionality assumption gives. Full credit: States the constant speed as 240 ÷ 3 = 80 km/h.
States the proportionality assumption the method depends on. Full credit: Explicitly assumes a constant speed before applying the ratio.
Sets up the correct proportion or scaling relation. Full credit: Sets up a correct relation, whether as 240/3 = d/7.5 or as 80 per hour scaled by 7.5.
Carries out the arithmetic correctly. Full credit: Both 80 km/h and 600 km are computed correctly.
Interprets the result in the problem's terms. Full credit: States that the car travels about 600 km in 7.5 hours at that constant speed.

q3.text: The car covers 80 km each hour because 240 divided by 3 is 80. So in 7.5 hours it goes 80 times 7.5, which is 600. It travels 600 kilometres.

results.feedback: Selected b, the only correct expression: the rate is flour per milk, 3/2.
Partial credit: TP=1, FP=0, c=2, i=2; score = 3 × (1×2 − 0×2) / (2×2) = "3/2" exactly, displayed 1.5. Option a is correct; option b (origin-crossing) is also correct and was not selected.
Correct rate and arithmetic, but the assumption is only implied and the interpretation omits the constant-speed condition.

criterion_scores.evidence: The car covers 80 km each hour because 240 divided by 3 is 80
criterion_scores.justification: States the constant speed explicitly and correctly.
A per-hour rate implies constant speed but the assumption is never stated.
Correct scaling of the unit rate by 7.5 hours.
The result 600 is correct, but 80 × 7.5 = 600 is asserted without showing the half-hour step the problem's 7.5 invites.
Interprets the number as a distance, though the constant-speed condition is left implicit.

assessment.title: Classics — Unit 08: The Lathe of Heaven — Final Exam
assessment.subject: Literature / Philosophy
assessment.instructions: Open-book, 60 minutes. Section B requires two of three essays; Section C requires one of two short answers. Read the section preambles for how many answers are required.

questions.prompt: In the novel, whose dreams alter reality?
Answer any two of the following three essays.

alternatives.prompt: On wu wei and Orr's agency: does the novel endorse quietism?
On Haber and the critique of utopian and technocratic engineering.
On the novel's ontology and its unstable reality.

questions.prompt: Answer one of the following two short answers.

alternatives.prompt: State the Daoist objection to Haber's improvements in one or two sentences.
State the novel's argument about who bears responsibility for an authored world.

a1.explanation: Orr's dreams change the world; Haber directs them.

b1.reference_answer: Quietism is the failure to act; wu wei is effective non-coercive action, and Orr acts through the dream rather than withdrawing from it.

criteria.description: States what wu wei requires of an agent, and what quietism would be. Full credit: distinguishes principled non-coercion from passivity.
Grounds the claim in specific episodes of the novel. Full credit: cites at least two episodes accurately.
Explains how the evidence supports the thesis without internal contradiction. Full credit: the argument's steps connect.

b2.reference_answer: Haber's engineering reduces political problems to technical ones, and the novel treats that reduction as the source of each catastrophe.

criteria.description: Identifies the technocratic reduction the novel criticizes. Full credit: names the reduction, not just Haber's ambition.
Grounds the critique in specific episodes of the novel. Full credit: cites at least two episodes accurately.
Explains how the evidence supports the thesis without internal contradiction. Full credit: the argument's steps connect.

b3.reference_answer: Reality in the novel is revisable and layered; the concurrences make the instability structural rather than a plot device.

criteria.description: States what the novel claims reality is. Full credit: distinguishes instability from mere illusion.
Grounds the claim in the concurrences and their consequences. Full credit: traces at least one continuity across revisions.
Explains how the evidence supports the thesis without internal contradiction. Full credit: the argument's steps connect.

c1.reference_answer: Centralized improvement imposes the improver's values and treats the beneficiaries as objects of a design rather than agents.

criteria.description: Names the Daoist objection to imposed improvement. Full credit: identifies coercion by a central planner.

c2.reference_answer: Responsibility falls on whoever directs the dream, since the world's revision is deliberate even when its details are not foreseen.

criteria.description: Locates responsibility for an authored world. Full credit: ties it to deliberate direction, not to unintended detail.

b1.text: Orr does not withdraw from the world; he revises it. Wu wei is action that does not coerce, and the dream is its instrument, so the novel's quietism is a charge it refuses. The misuse is Haber's, who treats each revision as an engineering task.

b2.text: Haber's improvements fail because he converts political questions into technical ones. Each fix removes one grievance and installs a new order of value that nobody chose, which is the novel's objection to the technical fix.

b3.text: The world of the novel is revisable and layered; what looks like an unstable reality is a reality with an author in it.

results.feedback: Selected b, the only correct option.

Three answers were provided for a two-of-three group; b1 and b2 are counted in the group's document order and b3 is ignored, not graded. b1 earned 30 of 35; b2 earned 55/2 of 35. The group maximum stays 70 (115/2 displays as 57.5).

criterion_scores.evidence: Wu wei is action that does not coerce
criterion_scores.justification: Distinguishes principled non-coercion from passivity, as the criterion requires.
Cites the dream and Haber's misuse; episode coverage is adequate but not rich.

criterion_scores.evidence: the novel's quietism is a charge it refuses
criterion_scores.justification: The steps connect, though the closing sentence asserts more than it shows.

criterion_scores.evidence: converts political questions into technical ones
criterion_scores.justification: Names the reduction rather than Haber's ambition, but hedges with 'improvements fail'.

criterion_scores.evidence: Each fix removes one grievance and installs a new order
criterion_scores.justification: Uses the novel's pattern accurately without citing a second episode.

criterion_scores.evidence: is the novel's objection to the technical fix
criterion_scores.justification: The argument's steps connect; the final clause restates rather than explains.

results.feedback: No alternative was answered, so the group earns 0 of 10. The group's maximum does not change with the answer sheet: the assessment is still marked out of 82.

assessment.title: Modern Israel and Palestine — Lecture 01 locator demo
assessment.subject: History
assessment.instructions: Answer both questions. Open book; citations in the key follow each source's declared locator scheme.

sources.note: Quotation attribution via the lesson passes. Print page ranges are not verified, so citations stay at chapter level; no invented page ranges.

sources.citation: Tessler, A History of the Israeli–Palestinian Conflict (1994)
Pipes, A History of the Middle East (1990)
Khalidi (ed.), From Haven to Conquest — course Reading booklet

sections.title: Section A — Short factual recall (5 pts)

questions.prompt: Which land-transfer pattern does Tessler describe for the first decade of Zionist settlement, and where does he place it?
Explain how the early Zionist leadership understood Arab opposition before 1914, and how that understanding changed. Ground the answer in the assigned readings.

a1.reference_answer: Settlement concentrated in coastal and inland colonies purchased on the market; Tessler places the pattern in the Ottoman period of Part I.

criteria.description: Names the land-transfer pattern. Full credit: market purchase under Ottoman land law, not confiscation.

b1.reference_answer: Before 1914 the leadership largely denied Arab national feeling and read opposition as economic or incited; the change tracks the Young Turk revolution and the early labour-Zionist encounters.

criteria.description: States how the leadership read Arab opposition, and what changed. Full credit: names denial of national feeling and gives the shift a cause.
Cites specific episodes or statements. Full credit: at least two, accurately attributed.

locators.note: Pipes reads the same episodes as a failed bargain; use only as a contrast.

criteria.description: Connects the evidence to the thesis without internal contradiction.

quote_verification.quote: in opposition to the will of the majority of the population
No solution! There is a gulf, and nothing can bridge it

quote_verification.note: Wording to confirm on the page pass; not used as scored evidence.

a1.text: Colonies were bought on the market rather than seized; Tessler puts it in the Ottoman Part I period.

b1.text: Before 1914 the leadership mostly denied that Arab opposition was national, reading it as the work of a few notables or as resentment of better farming. Morris's chapters on the second aliya show the shift beginning where labour Zionism ran into Arab labour.

results.feedback: Names the market-purchase pattern correctly and places it in the Ottoman period; the answer does not name the legal basis, so the criterion is partly earned.

criterion_scores.evidence: Colonies were bought on the market rather than seized
criterion_scores.justification: Names the pattern; Ottoman land law is not named, so full credit is not earned.

results.feedback: Denial of national feeling is named with a cause; two episodes are cited accurately, one only loosely. Coherence is sound but the closing sentence asserts more than it shows.

criterion_scores.evidence: the leadership mostly denied that Arab opposition was national
criterion_scores.justification: Names the denial and its cause in economic terms, as the criterion requires.

criterion_scores.evidence: Morris's chapters on the second aliya show the shift beginning
criterion_scores.justification: One episode is accurate and attributed; the second is gestured at rather than cited.

criterion_scores.evidence: the shift beginning where labour Zionism ran into Arab labour
criterion_scores.justification: The steps connect; the final clause is asserted rather than argued.

assessment.title: Modern Israel and Palestine — Lecture 01: Exam 01
assessment.subject: History
assessment.instructions: Answer every question. Section A is recall; Section B offers two essays — answer one.

segments.label: Lecture 01 — Background: Late Ottoman Palestine and the Origins of Zionism

scope.note: Required readings only. The optional-tier worksheet (WS02) is a separate assessment and does not gate.

sources.citation: Hertzberg (ed.), The Zionist Idea — Part 3 (Herzl) and Part 4 (Ahad Ha'am)
Avineri, The Making of Modern Zionism — Ch. 7 (Pinsker)
Laqueur, A History of Zionism — Chs. 1–3
Nordau, Speech at the First Zionist Congress (1897)

gate.note: Soft mastery — completion advances regardless of score (course policy).

questions.prompt: In Ahad Ha'am's 'The Jewish State and the Jewish Problem', what does he argue the Zionist movement must create?

options.text: A state with a Jewish majority as soon as possible
A spiritual centre in Palestine that shapes Jewish life in the Diaspora
A religious revival led by the rabbinate

questions.prompt: State Pinsker's diagnosis of the Jewish problem and the remedy he proposed.

sections.title: Section B — Analysis (10 pts)
sections.instructions: Choose ONE of the two essays.

alternatives.prompt: Explain how Laqueur's chapters 1–3 account for the emergence of political Zionism, and assess whether his account is compatible with Hertzberg's documents.
Using Avineri's chapter on Pinsker and Nordau's Congress speech, compare what each thought the movement was for.

assessed.note: Recall covers the Ottoman background and both readings' diagnoses; the essay group weighs the two framings.

omitted.topic: The 1936–39 Arab Revolt and its aftermath

coverage.note: Lecture 01 only; the optional-tier worksheet WS02 is a separate assessment and is not audited here.

q1.explanation: Ahad Ha'am's 'spiritual centre' is the reading's central claim; the political state is Herzl's programme, which he criticises.

q2.reference_answer: Pinsker reads Judeophobia as a hereditary, irrational fear that no emancipation can dissolve, and proposes a national territory secured by charter — a homeland, not necessarily Palestine.

criteria.description: Names the hereditary, irrational character of Judeophobia.
Names auto-emancipation: a territory secured by charter, with Palestine not required.

a1.reference_answer: Laqueur locates political Zionism in the failure of emancipation and of the forerunners, with Herzl as organiser; Hertzberg's documents supply the movement's own self-understanding — compatible at the level of diagnosis, not of programme.

criteria.description: States Laqueur's causal account: failed emancipation, forerunners, Herzl as organiser.
Weighs Hertzberg's documents against that account rather than summarising them.

a2.reference_answer: Avineri's Pinsker treats the problem as psychological and the remedy as a charter; Nordau's speech treats it as the physical and moral degeneration of the Western Jew, for which a state is the cure.

criteria.description: Pinsker: hereditary fear, charter territory.
Nordau: a degeneration diagnosis, the state as cure.

quote_verification.quote: in opposition to the will of the majority of the people, the community of nations has not yet learned to see in them anything but a horde of hated aliens
quote_verification.attribution: Pinsker, Auto-Emancipation (1882), as quoted by Avineri
quote_verification.note: Quoted inside Avineri's chapter; the original is not held.

q2.text: Pinsker says the fear of Jews is hereditary and cannot be cured by emancipation, so the remedy is a territory of their own, secured by a charter from the powers.

a2.text: Pinsker, on Avineri's reading, treats the problem as a psychological one: a fear carried by the host nation, answerable only by a charter for a territory. Nordau's Congress speech treats it as degeneration — the Western Jew is physically and morally marked by it — and so the cure is a state, not a refuge. The two agree that emancipation has failed, and differ on what the movement is for: a shelter or a reconstruction.

results.feedback: Correct. The 'spiritual centre' is the reading's claim, not Herzl's programme.
The diagnosis is exact; the remedy is named as a charter but Palestine is not excluded, as the criterion asks.

criterion_scores.evidence: the fear of Jews is hereditary and cannot be cured by emancipation
criterion_scores.justification: Both halves of the diagnosis are stated.

criterion_scores.evidence: the remedy is a territory of their own, secured by a charter
criterion_scores.justification: The charter is named; the reading's point that Palestine is not required is missing.

results.feedback: Both views are stated accurately and distinguished at the close. The comparison could weigh the two diagnoses against each other, which is what the second criterion asks.

criterion_scores.evidence: treats the problem as a psychological one: a fear carried by the host nation
criterion_scores.justification: The diagnosis and the charter remedy are both named.

criterion_scores.evidence: Nordau's Congress speech treats it as degeneration
criterion_scores.justification: The diagnosis is named; 'state, not a refuge' is stated.
